Doom: Here is a gun. Shoot everything.

As a psychological consultant, here's my professional opinion:

You angry? Play DOOM to let it all out.
You depressed? Play DOOM to feel satisfaction.
You shy? Play DOOM to gain confidence.
You fine? Play DOOM to feel even better.

Games don't cause violence. Go squash in some heads. Go blow off some steam. Have fun.

The single player campaign of Doom has exceeded all of my expectations I initially had toward it. My expectations were that I wanted it to be a great FPS game, and more importantly, a true DOOM title. I started the game on Nightmare difficulty right off the bat.

You will be fighting in the first 10 seconds of the game. Combat is challenging and very fluid with emphasis on speed, which they've certainly cranked up. Stopping is death on nightmare. Glory kills are satisfying, can be a ammo saver, and really don't hinder game flow at all, and can even be upgraded to perform faster (or toggled off in the options).

Level design is absolutely impressive. This was my biggest concern with Doom, and rest assured id FINALLY did it right. Non-linear, lots of exploration, plenty of secrets with hidden guns, secret level unlocks, and equipment.

The monsters are relentless. On nightmare you will get your ass kicked. This is a fact, and there's no way to circumvent this. I honestly felt at times that I was playing Project Brutality on "Last Man on Earth" difficulty. Monsters boast a variety of attacks, chase you down, flank you, and can be tough as nails (sometimes a little too good).

Weapons look and feel satisfying, great attention to detail. You will use guns interchangeably, each has their respective uses. You'll have to search the environment for health and ammo, aside from the chainsaw kills on enemies, they drop little items- but enough to keep you going (i.e +5 health occasionaly or like 4 shotgun shells). The BFG literally clears an entire room in one shot, and I couldn't help but smile at the results. Upgrades and progression in this game are entirely optional, but really help shift the game to fit how you play (the air control ability is the best imo).

The graphics are incredible too, although you better have a strong card if you want to play on Ultra with anti-aliasing, etc. Uncapping framerate, setting your FOV to 130, tons of options to customize.

And I have to say, Mick Gordon's soundtrack in this game is some of the best I've heard in a while. On the third level, I was literally head banging and rocking out to a soundtrack that felt like a crossbreed between Lamb of God, Celldweller, and Rage Against the Machine.

Overall, I can confidently say that this is the Doom game we've wanted. We all can breath a sigh of relief now that the main portion of the game is actually well-done. That beta we played is absolutely no indicator of how the campaign plays in the slightest, and id did it right with this one. Definitely recommend this title as a gamer, a die hard Doom fan (still play the classic to this day), and FPS fanatic.

EDIT: Since some of you do not take the time to actually explore the game's options and like to jump to conclusions, you can in fact start the game on nightmare. Ultra-nightmare is unlocked after beating the game, NOT regular nightmare. Fact.

BEST FPS OF THE DECADE.

DOOM 2016 is the smash-hit revival of the iconic "Father of FPS" series everyone thought had died with Doom 3. The hype was real, and boy did DOOM deliver. This game is both satisfying not only to long time fans of the series, but to new blood as well. Don't just take my word for it there; allow me to explain in depth why DOOM is worth your money.

[h1]The Positives[/h1]

[b][u]Holy optimization, Batman![/u][/b]
DOOM is the go-to game when I have to show somebody that modern games do not have to sacrifice flowing FPS and gameplay for the sake of pretty baubles and fancy textures. DOOM uses a rather unique form of rendering and AA that makes the game not fully render textures the player is not currently able to see or is far away from. The result is a small bit of loading-in that depends on your PC power, but the ability to have a remarkably consistent 30+ frames with NO drops, AT ALL TIMES. Even though my own computer (A laptop, no less) is about 5 years outdated, I can still run this at 30+ fps on medium settings, and it doesn't even look that bad. If you were worried you can't run the game, give it a shot. You might be in for a surprise.

[b][u]Intense, rewarding gameplay that stays true to the core mechanics of the originals[/u][/b]
Original fans of the series will remember the original games highly rewarded two things: Moving around to dodge attacks instead of hiding behind cover, and exploring every nook and cranny of the levels for early weapon unlocks and powerups. DOOM 2016 is not lacking at all in this regard. The game is fast, intense, and heavily favors mobile combat by completely removing all cover and making enemies super aggressive. Every shotgun to the face feels devastating as it rips chunks of flesh off your enemies and their bodies stumble to the ground. The game is also no slouch in the exploration department, with cleverly hid secrets like powerups and armor hidden around the map to find and exploit. In essence, DOOM feels just as good to shoot and explore as it did when it first came out. Maybe even better.

[b][u]The story is there, if you want it[/u][/b]
One of the more amusing aspects of DOOM is that the Doom Marine seems to care very little for anyone around him in his eternal quest to cause complete demon genocide. However, this new DOOM universe is actually quite rich and interesting. Lying around with the rest of the entertaining collectibles are data nodes that give you some quick information on where you are, who you are talking to, and what you are shooting at. A lot of it is very interesting information, and some is entertaining, but all of it is entirely optional for those who care about it. They didn't have to put this much effort into their world, but they did and it's pretty good stuff. I specifically enjoy how the Doom Marine is now considered to be something akin to a God of War by the demons, written in their legends as the most fearsome being ever known and having slaughtered millions of them before he was contained. That is hardcore.

[b][u]A fantastic amount of optional content[/u][/b]
DOOM 2016 has kept true to the old feel of the original Doom, but it has also added a good touch of new enjoyable features as well. This includes spaced out collectibles to find, upgrades for your weapons that are very, VERY satisfying to use, and Rune Trials, which are little fun challenges that unlock passive bonuses for the Doom Marine, like longer stun times and more ammo/health per pickup. It adds enough spice to not become overbearing, but to help further extend an already whopping 20+ hour campaign. 

[b][u]The Music[/u][/b]
This section is short and sweet. Mick Gordon did a stellar job at capturing the absolutely mental hardcore nature of DOOM with his soundtrack. It perfectly complements the gameplay and gets your blood pumping for more demon slaying.

[h1]The Negatives[/h1]

[b][u]The difficulty is kinda cheap at higher levels[/u][/b]
For better or worse, DOOM 2016 takes a page out of the original Doom's book in terms of difficulty increase. Except where the original game actually added more enemies per level and even changed some item locations, DOOM has the same amount of enemies with a flat and large damage increase to them, to the point where at Ultra-Violence and Nightmare a single Imp is more than capable of beating your face in with only two fireballs. Some players like this, and while I enjoy a good challenge (See my achievements in all three Dark Souls games), it gets tedious constantly being at 40 health and looking for more armor and health to lose again in the next fight with no other changes.

[b][u]Forgettable multiplayer[/u][/b]
While some people would enjoy it for this very reason, the multiplayer in DOOM is more reminiscent of Quake meets Halo than anything unique. I didn't play much (Admittedly because multiplayer just isn't my thing) but the only unique feature DOOM adds is the gimmicky Demon form, which is great to play as but annoying as hell to play against. Nothing really stands out that would make DOOM purchasing for the multiplayer over other popular options. Buy it for the campaign, not the online.

[b][u]Locked in place cutscenes[/u][/b]
In any other game this wouldn't even be mentioned, but it matters to DOOM. DOOM is all about frantic, fast-paced action and adrenaline at all times. Then abruptly the game will force you to not move for a minute or two. I don't mind exposition, in fact I LOVE the new world Bethesda and Id made, but forcing the player to suddenly stop dead takes you out of the action hard, like slamming on the brakes during a drag race. Its jarring and unpleasant, but thankfully doesn't last long and doesn't happen often. But when it does happen, it hurts.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
In essence, DOOM 2016 is an absolute blast, and a worthy modernization of the most iconic FPS game of all time. It promised, and it delivered. Sure, it has some negatives, but the positives far, far exceed them. Do yourself a favor and grab DOOM. I promise you won't regret it. I only paid $30 when this first came out on sale, and got 30 hours out of the campaign. If that's not cost effecient, I don't know what is.

At its best, Doom is everything it should be: a single-player campaign that’s just you, your super shotgun, and barely the amount of ammunition required to kill every single demon on Mars. It feels like a Doom game as you desperately try to find health pickups to keep you going, an ever-growing menagerie of demons snapping at your heels. It's exhausting and exciting and a little bit dumb, and when you're into it you're all the way in. At its worst, Doom is a repetitive series of enclosed rooms filled with demons, all of which you must kill to advance, complemented by a derivative and poorly thought-out multiplayer mode.
First impressions wise, Doom strikes all the right notes. The Union Aerospace Corporation's research facility on Mars runs red with the blood of employees who’ve learned a new meaning for the phrase 'wrongful termination,' but that barely matters to the inexplicably mute Doomguy, who shoots anything and everything which moves. Starting with only the pistol encourages you to focus on the diabolically delightful Glory Kill system — shoot your nearest Demon enough that they become staggered and highlighted in blue or orange, and if you press F (or R3 on a PS4 controller) while standing next to them you will rend them asunder. That is to say, you'll tear off their limbs and, in more than a few cases, joyfully beat them with their own appendages.

As someone with a degree in applied psychology, here's my professional opinion:

You angry? Play DOOM to let it all out.
You depressed? Play DOOM to feel satisfaction.
You shy? Play DOOM to gain confidence.
You fine? Play DOOM to feel [b]even better[/b].

Games don't cause violence. Go squash in some heads. Go blow off some steam. Have fun.

If you're looking for a game where you can punch demons in the face, surf on shotgun shells, and headbang to heavy metal while doing it — [b]DOOM[/b] is your new best friend.

Performance? Smoother than a buttered-up chainsaw. Graphics? Totally solid — not mind-blowing, but hey, you’re too busy splattering hellspawn to care.

Now let’s talk about enemies: these suckers are freaky, fun, and full of attitude. Special shoutout to my boy [b]Pinky[/b] — big, angry, and dumb as bricks. Love that guy.

The story’s there if you want it, but let’s be honest: you’re here to smash demons, not read a novel. And the game respects that; You don’t play DOOM for deep thoughts. You play it to turn demons into red mist.

Now the maps? Huge, layered, and loaded with secrets. You’re not just running hallways — you’re leaping across platforms, unlocking hidden rooms, and hunting collectibles. Every level is like a violent puzzle box with blood and metal. There’s even fast travel at the end of every level so you can go back and grab what you missed. Verticality, exploration, and brutal combat arenas — it's all here.

It’s fast. It’s loud. It’s metal.
[b]Highly recommended for anyone who thinks therapy should involve explosions.[/b]

It's an arena shooter.

I'm not kidding. You basically get locked inside of rooms filled with ammo, health, and usually a powerup or two. Demons spawn in order of ascending difficulty as grungy metal music kicks in, and you have to kill them to unlock the doors so you can walk down some corridors and head to the next arena. The game consists of doing this about 40 times. You very rarely get to navigate hostile terrain and pick off enemies from a distance like in retro Doom, and when you do, it's mostly just zombies. 

But hell, this game is [i]fun[/i]. It takes what worked from Doom 3, and replaces everything else with solid homages to the original Doom. The crazy colorful environments with cliffs and steep drops are back. The frantic fights with a dozen enemies at once are back. 

Interestingly, for the first time in Doom history, none of the enemies are given weapons with bullets (the chaingunners even fire energy spheres), meaning that you never have to hide behind cover and you can stay alive just by your dodging skills alone. 

Also, [i]there is no reload button[/i]. All your weapons automatically reload themselves and most don’t even have a cooldown, meaning you can just keep firing until you’re out of ammo. That’s about as awesome as it sounds.

Amazingly, someone must have realized that Hell was the best part of Doom 3, and this game sends you there not once, but [i]three times[/i]. I especially loved the ""Necropolis" level which was almost pure fanserivce to classic Doom in ways I don't dare spoil. 

But probably best of all, this game has some serious attitude and a sense of humor. Doomguy is a destroyer of worlds, and you can feel his aggression in all of his actions even though you only see him through his own eyes, thanks in no small part to glory kills.

I found that the notorious “glory kills” while odd at first, worked to the game’s advantage. For those who don’t know, when an enemy is almost dead, they can be finished off with a single flamboyant melee attack which will also spew a fountain of health pickups into the air.  Not only do they humorously show off Doomguy’s rage, but they aren’t really all that new [strike]since they were ripped straight from Brutal Doom[/strike]. In retro Doom, you’d have to run over dead bodies to collect the ammo drops, and it wasn’t unusual to give the enemies a punch or a grind with the chainsaw to conserve a little ammo. Glory kills are basically that, but just happen to make it look a bit cooler. They become a bit less important in the second half of the game, as the game starts throwing you into some ridiculous situations and you’ll probably just want to blast enemies to smithereens without worrying about carefully whittling down their health. 

I give Doom 4 an 8 / 10. If you were hoping for the true return of classic Doom, I’ve got news for you: nothing is going to be like classic Doom. If you want classic Doom, go play that. ZDoom.org is on your right, Doomworld.com is on your left. Truth is that classic Doom never left; source ports exist which can add dynamic lighting and make the game look ridiculously modern, and the community is still alive and pumping out dozens of new maps and mods every week. But after the strange horror/corridor shooter that was Doom 3, Doom 4 returns the series to its roots in the best way possible: it will transport you to a colorful world of sprawling martian compounds and hellscapes, a place where you never need to stop running at full speed, a place where it just feels good to pull the trigger and watch hundreds of imps and mancubi crumble before you.

Barely any story, generic rooms filled with the same enemies, a shitton of heavy metal music blasting in your ears, no reloading.....

Yeah, if this isn't DOOM, I don't know what is.

Before starting this review, I'd like to just point out that I never was a fan of ultra-violent/gory games. I have played the original Doom, and while the older graphics made the "violence" factor bearable, I never really got much enjoyment out of it due to the fact that I tend to get motion sickness with older FPS games, sadly. I never had any intentions of playing 2016 DOOM, but I ended up buying it on a whim during a sale. I never expected to get as much enjoyment from it as I actually did.

Story - I never expected the story to be anything mindblowing. In the general sense, it's not. With the premise of the game being what it is, however, the story is pretty awesome. Id was able to create a smooth, interesting narrative with the use of only 3 characters (not including the silent protagonist). The campaign took me around 10 hours to beat and I felt it was the perfect length for the kind of game it is. Some people may take longer if they choose to hunt for collectibles on the first go, or end up dying a lot. I believe it had a perfect balance between story dialogue and actual gameplay, as I never once felt like any one part was dragged out for too long. I won't go into detail about specific plot points for spoiler reasons, but I will say that [spoiler]Olivia Pierce and Samuel Hayden can go **** themselves.[/spoiler] All in all, it's still the basic premise of the original DOOM -- A man bent on killing every last demon from hell. As a bonus, there's a great amount of lore to be read based on certain collectibles and/or interacting with certain enemies and objects and it's all fairly interesting, especially for fans. ~ 8/10

Gameplay - The pace of combat seems to be fairly on par with the original DOOM. It's frantic and at times can be a bit overwhelming, especially when playing on higher difficulties. It literally took 10 seconds after the game started to kill the first enemy. It wastes no time in throwing you straight into the action, which is what DOOM stands for. "Glory Kills" are something new that was very controversial to many who deem themselves DOOM purists. However, I personally think it's a cool concept and was executed well. It not only works as an aesthetic design choice, but also to help you conserve ammunition on weapons. The level design sticks to its original formula, where it has a Metroidvania style of exploration, though not nearly as difficult to find your way around as the original games (thanks to objective markers). Nonetheless, the levels themselves are pretty solid and well-designed. Lastly, the movement is very fluid and fast-paced; which is important if you wanna keep your distance from enemies, or run up to them and blast them in the face. >:) ~ 9/10

Graphics/Art Style - In short, it looks great. The dark atmosphere is captured extremely well; from the subtle lighting effects, to the blood smears across the walls and floors. Enemy death animations during "glory kills" are a sight to behold. They're gruesome and they look fantastic. On the subject of enemies --- They are absolutely terrifying. The attention to detail on their models are fantastic and it's awesome to see what the original DOOM demons look like in full 3D/HD. (Nice to see that Cacodemons are not actually flying meatballs).  Don't expect anything vibrant from this game though. As I said, DOOM is a dark game with a dark atmosphere, and from a graphical standpoint, it looks good. From an art style perspective, it's gloomy, which is the whole point. ~ 9/10

Soundtrack - I'll be honest, I prefer the soundtrack of the original DOOM over this. Now don't get me wrong here. I find the soundtrack of the reboot to be totally kick-A$$ as well. It may just be a weird sense of nostalgia taking over. The original DOOM soundtrack has become such a staple of video game culture, that's it's hard to think of any other DOOM soundtrack improving on it. With that said though, the music still fits very well with the game and the action in general. The "metal" influences can be heard throughout, just like with the original. By the way, I don't know where else to put this but I just want to point out that for the most part, the demons' wails and screams sound pretty terrifying.  ~ 8.5/10

Multiplayer - I didn't expect too much from multiplayer, but I was pleasantly surprised with the variety of game modes available (which consist of classic FPS game modes like Capture the Flag and Team Deathmatch, as well as new interesting "DOOM exclusive" modes) and how fun it is in general. It's nothing to write home about, but it is worth checking out and does provide some hours of enjoyment. It's generally fast-paced and does have a sizeable player base for now. Of course, it isn't for everyone and after a while it does tend to get somewhat dull. You can customize your character in multiplayer by obtaining customization items that are unlocked when reaching a certain level or completing specific challenges. Before the free DLC update, you could just equip whatever was included in the DLC right away. Now, they're locked (in most cases) behind a huge grind... which sucks. The game also includes a feature called SnapMap, which is basically a glorified level editor. You can share your levels with other players and vice versa. I can see the appeal, and while there are some cool user created levels out there, it's mostly a gimmick and is by no means a game seller.  ~ 6/10

Replay Value - With an 11 hour campaign on average and lots of collectibles to be found, this game has a great amount of replay value. If not only for the collectibles, but also for just how fun the gunplay is. Many will want to go through DOOM guy's journey to hell and back all over again. Ultra Nightmare difficulty is unlocked after beating the game once, which is hell (no pun intended). There's an achievement tied to beating it on that difficulty, so achievement hunters, you'll get a kick out of this. There's also an arcade mode which lets you replay levels from the campaign as you aim to get a high score. I highly recommend it for the enthusiasts. ~ 9/10

In short, this is a fantastic game for people who are already established fans of the DOOM franchise and people who enjoy FPS and/or gory games and holds a great amount of replay value. This is one of the rare exceptions for FPS games where I recommend getting it for the single-player. The multiplayer is just a neat little bonus which may or may not appeal to you.

[b]Final Score ~ 8.5/10[/b]

[b] Doom (2016) - A bow to one's own past[/b]

You could write so much about Doom that it would be enough for a book. From questionable decisions, backstories to confusing naming, Doom has it all.
Luckily, id Software has decided not to continue using the number in the title because the game, like Doom Eternal and Doom 3, is a reboot of Doom. And as is almost usual with Doom, opinions about the game are very divided among many fans. The days of sneaking through dark rooms armed with a flashlight and being surprised by demons are over. Doom 3 wasn't a bad game, but for many it just didn't feel like a real Doom.
The reboot was intended to revitalize the concept of classic and fast shooter action and bring it back into the mainstream. Whether that's the game or id software that succeeded?

[b]I only play Doom because of the story…[/b]

... but of course that's nonsense and it doesn't really matter to me when it comes to Doom, but the story they've come up with here is more complex than you think.

I won't reveal anything more than "people are once again fiddling with something they shouldn't have been fiddling with, a portal to hell opens on Mars and demons are killing all the employees and want more..." because who If you follow the monologues and read the codex entries, you will get enough insight into the story. If you don't feel like it or want to know beforehand, you can read a summary of the story in the comments to my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/omn1cron/recommended/782330/]Doom Eternal Review[/url].

[b]Back to the roots [/b]

After just a few minutes you notice that this part is different.
The first weapon and enemies follow seconds after the game starts and the terminal, from which an unknown voice is about to start talking about the situation and the mission, is quickly ripped out of its holder and thrown into the corner.
Our hero isn't in the mood for idle chatter and we know what it's all about anyway. There are always little bits of action and one or two monologues, but if you don't listen, you won't miss much.

No hesitation, no pauses, a short logo and it starts immediately with a powerful sound.

While most shooters force the player to walk at a leisurely pace and are stingy with sprint endurance, the Nameless Space Marine is breathtakingly fast.
Modern elements such as regenerating energy, cover systems or simple reloading are fortunately missing, as are annoying NPCs standing around in the way.
The game does not rely on a subtle horror atmosphere like its direct predecessor, but on pure adrenaline.

The initially narrow and linear space station corridors are deceptive, because the core of the gameplay is the arena battles against a variety of very agile hellish creatures and the new central element: the "Glory Kills".
The numerous arguments are not particularly imaginative, but they are extremely exciting. The arenas and the amount of agile opponents force you to stay in constant motion.
It has always been clear that the game is not a rainbow unicorn children's birthday party because without the sometimes exaggerated gore effects it wouldn't be the game it is and the new Glory Kills put the crown on the previously known splatter.
Cliff Blezinski, the father of Gears of War, commented on the Glory Kills in a tweet with "My only small criticism is the same one I have with my old games: don't focus so much on the execution animations." However, the difference is that in Gears of War this was purely an end in itself, but in Doom it is an elementary part of the game mechanics.

The visually slightly intrusive and sometimes nonsensical positions of floating neon green armor or ammunition or health packs standing in corners could certainly have been integrated more homogeneously into the game and, as in other games, could have been gray and placed in cupboards or on corpses.
But exactly this representation is pure intention because, on the one hand, it is a nod to the past and, on the other hand, a realistic representation or placement of these elements would counteract the flow of the game.

[b]id Software has managed to rip the heart out of the old games and put it into a modern and contemporary engine.[/b]

And you can find that everywhere in the game. Be it the level design and the associated collection stuff, which not only refers to the obligatory key cards, without which it is often impossible to progress. In addition to the small naval dolls, there are access to old classic maps from Doom and Doom 2, mega health bubbles, Argent cells that permanently improve the standard values and combat support drones that make it possible to unlock weapon modifications as well as small extra levels in the form of rune tests equip ourselves with perks.
Some of this collectible stuff can be found directly, but a lot of it has to be searched for in the complex levels. And that's almost as much fun as the quick arena battles.
But no worry. If you don't want to do the collecting stuff or the rune tests, you can get to the end without all of that.

For me, the game is a completely successful rebirth of a classic that is characterized neither by boring citations nor nostalgic winks and is a successful transfer of the spirit of the original into the present.
The simplicity, speed and harshness of the forefather was catapulted into the present shows that not everything left behind by the “evolution” of the genre is obsolete.
Even if the breakneck speed of Quake is not quite reached, the game is still entertaining and refreshing and the fact that there is no sequel number adorning this title is no coincidence because: 

[b]Doom is back[/b] and neither wants to stage a believable world nor convey the drama of a military operation, let alone tell a profound story.

Doom is an entertaining and action-packed game and uncompromisingly subordinates everything to this goal.

[h1]DOOM.[/h1]
[i]RIP AND TEAR!

*This is solely a review of the campaign.[/i]

[b][u]Introduction[/u][/b]
DOOM (2016) is, perhaps, the best [i]traditional[/i] FPS of all time. I realize this is absurdly high praise, but I don’t think it’s unwarranted. DOOM is the resurrection of a truly all-out, balls-to-the-wall, gore-filled shooter that focuses entirely on just that – the shooting. Every design detail, every choice ID software made in the development of this game, was chosen expressly for the purpose of making the act of ripping and tearing apart Demons from Hell more entertaining and bas-a$s. There’s something about the purity of that that’s impossible not to love. In DOOM, you are an unrestricted cavalcade of death and destruction. If you like the sound of that, read on: it only gets better.

[b][u]”Plot”[/u][/b]
I want us to tear into the meaty bits of DOOM ASAP, so I’ll set the stage in four more sentences. You are the Doom Slayer. You are driven by an insatiable rage to eviscerate, shoot, explode, pulverize, and generally rip every last demonic entity limb from limb. You are currently on a Mars space station where hubristic men have opened a portal to Hell, and demon spawn is spewing forth. [i]Time to f*cking rip and tear, Doom Slayer.[/i]

[b][u]Presentation & Aesthetic[/u][/b]
Of all the AAA games released on PC in the second half of the 2010’s, DOOM may hold the title for the best graphical-fidelity-to-performance-ratio. Every aspect of the visuals are stellar, from the textures to the lighting; and the animations to the special effects. All of DOOM’s environments are immaculately rendered, their realism only making the grotesque hellscapes of the levels that much more disturbing. Compound this striking visual quality with the even more impressive stability of its performance, and you have a real winner. But, if the god-tier graphics, aesthetic, and performance aren’t enough for you, there’s still the soundtrack – which is an absolute masterpiece. It’s not that any one track is extremely memorable (though some are), it’s that the score is almost entirely heavy metal, which is gloriously apt ambiance as you cut a demon in half with a chainsaw. Nuff’ said. DOOM’s presentation is near unparalleled by any game this generation.

[b][u]Weapons & Combat[/u][/b]
You can’t have a good FPS without a top-notch arsenal, and DOOM’s got you covered. There are eight base weapons in the game, nearly all of which have two earnable weapon modifications to further their utility and enjoyment. There are also two more special weapons, the chainsaw and BFG (Big F*cking Gun). Each have their own unique way of vaporizing, detonating, or mincing Satan-spawn; which is excellent, as gunplay variety is one of DOOM’s greatest achievements. If this vast ordinance isn’t doing it for you, don’t worry, there’s more! Every enemy in the game, after being weakened enough, can be finished off with a glory kill, a sort of crème de la crème butchering animation. Glory kills include, but are not limited to: ripping a demon’s jaw off, snapping their neck, exploding their skull, and ripping their arm off to bludgeon their face with. Don’t ask, it just works. 

[b][u]Demons & Locations[/u][/b]
Moving on to where the Doom Slayer applies his veritable armory of weapons, there are roughly a dozen normal enemy types; but very few are describable as cannon fodder. On proper difficulty, every demon represents a terrible beast to overpower, and that’s exactly what fighting a resident of Hell should be. Making matters better, each type will challenge you in a different way, forcing the player to think quickly on their feet; culminating in transforming them into a multitasking symphony of carnage once they get the hang of things. There’s no greater show of your accumulated skills than through any of the boss battles though, which test your mastery of the weaponry; and your ability to strafe, respond to new attacks, and land precise strikes. All these battles occur in the set dressing of either industrial Mars or the depths of Hell – fitting locations for a warm bloodbath.

[b][u]Upgrades & Power-Ups[/u][/b]
Now that I’ve paid my dues to the visceral sides of combat, I should give a rundown of the more technical component. There are several upgrades and power-ups to attain throughout the campaign to make the Doom Slayer just that much more effective in slaughter. These entail weapon tokens earned through various methods which allow you to super-charge the power of your weapon modifications, praetor tokens which upscale your armor to be more effective in several ways, and a few rare argent cells which will increase either your max health, max armor, or max ammo carrying capacity. On top of this there are also rune challenges which, when completed, give the player a unique passive ability if equipped. Finally, there are also pickups which give you a timed power-up, such as quadrupled damage, or invulnerability. These gameplay elements marginally detract from the simplicity of the carnage, but do add welcome gameplay variation.

[b][u]Breakneck Pace[/u][/b]
Before I finish talking about the magnificent gameplay, I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention possibly its most vital element: the speed. As you engage with each successive demon horde, you’ll very quickly learn that to stop moving is equivalent to death. The game forces you to move nonstop in every combat sequence – navigating hallways, jumping across platforms, and crisscrossing the entire given arena. DOOM supports this gameplay technique doubly by making the Doom Slayer extremely fast on his feet, his weapons self-reloading, and his glory kills as quick as they are brutal. The hastened pace of DOOM’s gameplay magnifies the game’s difficulty and excitement. I wouldn’t have it any other way.

[b][u]”Story”[/u][/b]
As the past four paragraphs on detailed gameplay design can attest, DOOM is much more focused on blood-pumping gameplay than any sort of frilly narrative. There is, nevertheless, a barebones storyline occurring parallel to the Doom Slayer’s massacres. I can’t really say I understood it in its entirety (I was a bit too carried away in the bloodlust), but the jist is that men were harnessing energy from Hell through shoddy methods, when finally someone snapped and released the demons into our dimension. You go through the game killing Hell spawn and closing portals, often at the behest of Samuel Hayden; the nine-foot tall robot running the Mars facility. The story is nothing special and is easily ignored, which is entirely fine – even desirable – for a DOOM game.

[b][u]Legacy[/u][/b]
As a final note, I should mention just how significant DOOM (2016) is for the gaming industry. DOOM (1993) was [i]the[/i] game that popularized the FPS genre. However, following the release of DOOM 3 and its lack of success, the death of the traditional FPS was all but cemented. What followed was a procession of cover-shooters, looter-shooters, modern warfare games, and otherwise gimmicky titles. That DOOM (2016) re-emerged to reclaim its throne as a trend-setting FPS, to wide commercial acclaim, is a miraculous turn of events for everyone that likes fast-paced fun and challenge in their FPS games. Daddy DOOM spawned a lot of offspring, but when he saw them to be inadequate for his mantle, he picked up his super-shotgun and showed them what’s what.

[b][u]Conclusion[/u][/b]
For all my descriptions and characterizations, you really have to experience DOOM for yourself to understand its unrivaled allure. There’s nothing more blood-rushing, masculine, and awe-inspiring than disemboweling a fifteen-foot Demon with your bare hands. That’s just not something you get to do every day, and it’s not something any video game has ever let you do in such a well realized way. There is no FPS better than DOOM (2016) for pure, visceral butchery. Well, except maybe soon, [i]DOOM Eternal…[/i]

This game is the definition of ultimate badassery. You are the legendary Doom Marine. You awaken from your ancient slumber and the first thing you do is you break off the chains from your arms with your godly strength and crush the skull of the first unlucky demon. Rip & Tear.

Coming from the gods of FPS, id Software, is a reboot infinitely more successful than the third installment. It exchanges the slower pace and horror focus of the third game for insane speed, velocity and verticality of combat. There is no time for cheap jump scares here. The game still maintains a solid horror or terror atmosphere with all the gore, pentagrams and demonic inscription scribbled along the walls of Union Aerospace and Hell.

What will strike your eyes first is the unprecedented and almost perfect use of user interface. It is so cool, natural, versatile and lovely with all of that clean graphical reactivity. It makes killing enemies more satisfying when you have a unique dynamically changing crosshair for each weapon. And there are many weapons, each having two obtainable modifications and those modifications have upgradable properties and masteries, creating a ton of combinations and possibilities that you sometimes forget you have them all.

Another wonderful asset of this game is its Codex. It was so much fun to read as it unlocks new entries after collecting data logs, weapons and killing enemies. It offers rich backstory information written in hard sci-fi lingo describing the science behind the demons, weapons, demonic mythology, harvesting of Argent energy and the corrupt UAC conduct and policies. This might sound boring but it's super interesting to read about, for example, the transference of consciousness of the dying CEO Dr. Samuel Hayden into a three meters tall cyborg. One can only wonder what we will be capable of in 2143, minus the siphoning of energy from the portals of Hell, of course.

Minus all of this story stuff, the core gameplay is fun as hell. Each enemy can be killed in a glorious finishing animation and with all the weapons, mods and runes the combat is never ever boring or repetitive. It takes some getting used to, especially the movement speed and parkour, but it was refreshing to see such a multi-layered level design.

The game contains an advanced map and a vast collectibles and secrets system that actually rewards you for locating secret areas with weapon upgrade points. This offers a ton of replayability. Dr. Samuel Hayden sounds a bit like Lance Henriksen and the facility's announcement system sounds like GLaDOS. The soundtrack is a legend. The optimization is amazing given how good the game looks. 

The game is awesome af. 'Nough said. Buuut, the overall impression and impact on myself is...

9/10

+ ripping and tearing demon body parts, amazing sleek interface, godly soundtrack, graphical maturity and optimization, rich hard sci-fi setting, story and lore, cool and badass, sufficiently long and replayable (not rating the multiplayer)
- the speed takes some getting used to, physically exhausting

I finally got around to playing doom.  After 25 years of waiting, I'm blown away by what people could do in the 90s with graphics technology at the time. 

Oh of course this isn't the original doom, and of course I've played Doom MANY times on many different systems.  But I also did grow up in the 80s and 90s and gave Doom to me as an impressionable child of only 12.   And ignoring what Jack Thompson would spout for years later I grew up to be a game developer and not a murderer.   Doom was one of those revolutionary games. 

24 years later, Doom came out again, the original team is no longer at ID but... if we grabbed that team and transported magically through time, Doom would probably look, play, and perhaps feel the same as this game.  And it's really DAMN brilliant. 

If I tried to sell a company on "DOOM" as it is, and called it anything else, I think I would be laughed out of an office.  A FPS where the story isn't the focus.  Where it's just room after room of fighting the same enemies, simple weapons that were made 20 years ago, and just the most ultra violence I could make. 

The thing is, DOOM is a game you can't make any more for all those reasons, it's probably TOO violent, it's mostly simplistic, and it's repetitive.    But this isn't any game, this is a vitalization of a franchise that started the genre and honestly anything but what this game is, would be a crime.  

There's really too many brilliant things to mention.  There is a story, but it's clear through action (not words) the main character isn't having any of it.  There's repetation but my god the action is INTENSE that even going through the same enemies thirty or forty times is intense.  Even the gameplay is run and gun, not "War run and gun" But this is DOOM classic run and gun.  An attack is coming at you?  Move out of the way.  Do that again and again and return fire and that's honestly a bit of brilliance in the modern era.  Raycasted bullets are the standard, but dear god, this breaks that mold. 

Then there's the violence, and it's QUITE over the top, but you know what? You're fighting demons from hell, using all sorts of weapons on them, and while the violence is visceral and in your face, it fits with the game's themes. 

There's the fact you fight enemies over and over, but this is a masterclass in level design.  The enemies have a good variety, but change slowly, the locations though are always epic, and you feel awesome ducking behind different areas, and seeing different elements of level design come into play, like the verticality and circular levels.   It's really exceptionally well done, something Romero would only have been able to dream of all those years ago. 

There's just a solo problem with the entire game, and that's the music.   E1M1 (At Doom's gate) is a masterpiece of audio that may not have been topped in video games, it gets you ready, puts you in the fight and gets your blood pumping, just listening to is just so awesome.

New Doom however.  The music isn't "bad" but there's definitely a lacking edge to this music and it's the single area that the game hasn't topped the original, but being unable to top a masterpiece isn't a horrible problem.  And while the music might not live up to it, the entire rest of the game gives with both barrels. 

There's Snapmap, and multiplayer and while snap map is interesting as an experiment, and multiplayer is decent, I didn't really feel a reason to return to either of them even with the improvements.  What you want to do here is play Doom, the most excellent of retro shooters, perhaps the only game that should be this retro and does so with the perfect style. 

But to be honest, this is a game that's going to be retro, and I really wish everyone could and would enjoy it.  The fact is much of this game is a return to form of a 25 year old game, however gaming has moved on in those 25 years, yet every "return to form" is exactly that.  It's returning to the great old days, not the rose tinted nostalgia days that were "better back then" but it returns us to what was great about those days and makes us glory in it. 

So while not every single person will like it (Some people will never be able to accept the super fast pace action), I can't do anything BUT recommend this game as to me I'd call it the perfect sequel to Doom.    And god I can't wait for the next one. 

Just please don't call the next one Doom 2, it's confusing enough calling this one DOOM.

I probably remember it wrong, but I once read one of those stories of game design ingenuity about the original Quake, about how when you fire the rocket launcher, the missile actually spawns right behind you, because it turns out to optimize both game performance and the felt rhythm of play. 

DOOM (2016) pulls this kind of tricks all the time. The game will snap you a small distance in space to make you feel and look good, giving you that last inch to grab a ledge, or letting you activate a finishing move at the last possible second, right when you most need the health boost it dispenses. Jonathan Blow talks about "generosity" as a design value, when you take a player gesture or affordance that might typically be kept scarce to make it exciting (such as time rewinds in Prince of Persia) and make it available all the time. DOOM is not a comprehensively generous game: it understands the micro-narrative impact of running out of railgun rounds two-thirds through a fight and having to revise your tactics in response (or taking a different approach on the next reload). But it is generous about the core experience of dancing around and shredding up hellspawn: you always have a shot, and it always look sick as shit. 

This game is at its best when I'm on my fifth try at a particular sequence and I'm reminding myself to just move fast and never stop. I know this song, after all.

Doom 2016 (Opinion)

The first Doom was my back up game in 1999, actually it was the only game my poor PC could play at the time. That and Wolfenstein. Let’s not forget my dad’s Age of Empire which he plays to this day. While everybody was busy exploring Black Mesa and PS 1 great array of games at the time, all I had was Doom. And Wolfenstein.  With that being said, it sure was pure frantic fun blowing demons back to where they once came from. From the standout fast pace shooting and the ridiculous secrets you can find, the original Doom 1 and 2 was game I could always run to. Despite getting bored occasionally from playing it too many times, it was always fun to use the chainsaw or the BFG wiping everything out including my stress from classroom. 


Summary
Playing it in 2018, I am pretty surprise that it’s pretty much the same game that keeps the same frantic shooting spree and ludicrous premise. And it’s definitely better for it. Obviously there have been new additions like glory kills and improvements done but it sort of throws away the horror elements that it was in Doom’s 3 reboot emphasising on adrenaline pumping first person action of old instead. This new 2016 DOOM starts with a bang, with the marine or Doomguy being strapped to some sort of altar and soon attacked by what I assume is zombies but apparently they are called the possessed. You are very soon creating carnage with melee kills and the pistol while exploring the Union Aerospace Corporation (UAC) which has been attacked. I was expecting a shooting and violence galore from what I gather from friends and reviews which it is but was still surprise by the developers when it came to world building and lore of Doom. There have been some added depth to the lore of creatures and this world through its codex as well as various exposition cut scenes. The plot is as generic as it could get. Really it’s about you stopping the forces of hell from coming over and the UAC from taking Hell energy to save Earth energy crisis. How many twist can you add to that kind of plot really but it’s delivered quite well especially the person who voiced Dr Samuel Hayden. The real blast of DOOM however is sending all these critters back to their hellhole anyway you see fit. Most of the time by shooting everything that moves and it does that like its 1993.   

Detail Overall

DOOM’s shooting is as solid as it was in 1993 (Well for me it would have been 1999), strafing left and right firing away. It almost feel like you are constantly being pump with adrenaline. Over the course of the 8 to 12 hour campaign, you will be using an array of weapons to dispatch your enemies. From the iconic super shotgun to such classics like the plasma rifle and rocket launcher. Gone are the present day shooters of holding two fire arms, here you will be able to carry all your fire arms like Rambo. The weapons are a great blast to use and there is level of depth to using each of them depending on the layout or the amount enemies thrown at you. What makes it more fun is experimentation of these weapons. Almost all of them has an alternative firing mode and they are blast to experiment. The heavy assault rifle missile pod firing is like a rocket launcher chain gun once it’s upgraded to its maximum capabilities. While the plasma rifle has an alternative firing mode that allows you to stun enemies allowing you to use new strategies to attack your enemies. The addition of challenges to upgrades weapon mods to its final capacity is also extremely rewarding like sniping head shots on Hell knights. It almost feel like Bloodborne finishing a boss bottle. 

Of course the most important addition is the glory kills mechanic. When enemies get stunned you are able to perform a glory kill that provides health, which creates a new strategy for some desperate attempt for a second breath when you are low on health. The glory kill animation are pretty good and different for all enemies. It also depends on which body parts you are looking at but it is satisfying (a bit funny too) tearing an imps arm and whacking it with its own arm. However they do get repetitive by the 6th or 7th hours of shooting and tearing limbs. I have heard comments that this mechanic slows the game down but personally I don’t think it does though. The chainsaw and BFG takes a somewhat different approach though now. They have limited ammo and the chainsaw kills provides ammo which becomes quite important in later stages when ammo gets a bit scarced.     

Level design is pretty good and varied with secret areas as well as Easter eggs for fans of the series. Such as introducing classic maps and Doom guy dolls. The inclusion of classic maps is also pretty cool for newcomers who want to experience a bit of gaming history pioneer in FPS. The enemy design is good because they look great being transported from 1993 to 2016 especially the Cacodemon and Pinky. They still have a lot of their original design and they looked absolutely gorgeous now. The pinky now have some upgrades as well as they heavily armoured in front but weak from behind. The boss fights are remarkably thrilling, asking to use all of your weapons and platforming abilities. Yes this new DOOM has some platforming and for the most part it works quite well. DOOM can get a bit easy at times but playing at ultra-violence adds some difficulty to master. Lastly the music is excellent from the ominous dread to synth wave heavy metal music, the music flows remarkably well with its combat. I wish steam included the soundtrack with my purchase.

The inclusion of an arcade mode and multiplayer is icing on the cake. However I have heard that the weakest part of DOOM is its multiplayer, I have yet to test it. The ability to create maps is another bonus allowing for some creative level design experimentation. At the end of the day DOOM is a blast to play because in so many ways it plays like the DOOM of old with some great additions. Of course better graphics too. Its emphasis on single player is also a plus, yay no micro transactions to disrupt me. DOOM is definitely buy for FPS fans and especially for those who grew up with it. Watching all your favourites enemies brought to life with today’s graphics is awesome. The barons of hell towering figure while it throws that green flame at you is still a blast to watch. Overall DOOM was worth it. Ohhhh that satisfying super shotgun.

A year later, I'm still using my old LGA775 PC with 3ghz q9650 oc'ed at 3.7ghz and 8gb of ram. [h1]DOOM (2016) - First Impressions (No Nostalgia)[/h1]

I went into Doom (2016) with zero nostalgia - this is my first Doom game - so I think my perspective is pretty objective.

I’m currently on Mission 8, and yeah… it’s fun. You just jump in and start destroying everything. It’s simple on the surface, and that’s exactly why it works. Good combat, fun challenges, and the game flows really nicely.

I get why people love it so much. The soundtrack is great, gameplay feels smooth, and even though it’s constant action, it doesn’t feel overwhelming or tiring. It’s actually kind of relaxing to play after a long day, which is weird to say about a game like this, but it’s true.

[b]But I do think it’s a bit overrated, especially without nostalgia.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]What I Didn’t Like[/h2]

One of my biggest issues is the level design - not in terms of visuals or effort, but in how it treats completionists. The game is actually pretty punishing if you’re trying to get everything. You often have to backtrack a lot, and in many later levels, you simply can’t return to certain areas. If you miss something, that’s it - you’ll have to replay the mission.

I get that replayability was probably the goal, but some people just want to finish the game and move on, especially when it’s linear and a second playthrough doesn’t add much beyond increased difficulty.

Achievements make it even worse. The game is clearly singleplayer-focused, but it still has multiplayer achievements. So if you want 100%, you’re forced into multiplayer or into finding people just to grind them. It doesn’t feel rewarding, just annoying.

The map is… fine. The 3D design makes sense because of vertical levels, but it’s not very helpful. No minimap, no quick orientation - you just keep opening it over and over. I get that some people enjoy memorizing levels and navigating just by memory, but not everyone plays like that, and it gets annoying having to constantly reopen the map. You do get used to it after a few missions, but early on it’s kinda frustrating.

The menu has a small but weird issue too. Pressing Tab doesn’t always open the map - it opens whatever you last obtained, like upgrades or lore. Not a huge deal, but it messes with the flow more than it should.

As for bugs, there aren’t many, but the ones that exist stand out. I’ve run into issues like not being able to shoot or having to restart a mission because a door wouldn’t open. For a game this popular, it’s surprising that some of these problems still exist after so many years.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Overall, it’s still a really good game. It does fast, satisfying action extremely well. But once you look past all the hype, there are definitely some design choices that feel outdated or just frustrating - especially if you’re trying to fully complete it.

[b]It’s great, just not perfect like people often say.[/b]

I cannot imagine anyone still reading reviews for this game. You either already have it, or you decided not to buy it for whatever strange reason.

Nonetheless, this game is great. Not to overuse the popular metaphors, but it is a great contrast to current conventional "grounded" shooters. 
You are literally a murderous monster with one desire - to kill demons. 

You are so successful at fulfilling that desire that legions of demons have legends of you and run scared when they see you. 

Your name is carved into ancient stone and industrial rock music emanates from the air as you walk the earth.

And boy is it a design marvel... the music responds to gameplay just fluidly enough so that you get into a rhythm that clicks well with shotgun reloads and bunnyhop timings.

There are a handful of videos online discussing the AI in the game - it is ingenuis. Long story short - the AI in the game is designed to literally be the opposite of cover based shooting. Every cover is a corner to die in, every moment of hesitation is punished by increased enemy accuracy.

Yes, the game is a string of repetitive formulaic arenas.
Yes, the narrative is a little forced over gameplay.
Yes, exploration is advantageous at the expense of gameplay pacing.

But holy-freaking-heck is it an enjoyable experience... Completed it three times by now. Will come back again to rip terrified imps in half with bare hands.
Very nice, family-friendly, Christian game. I highly recommend it!

I played this four years late to the party, but man... what a party this was!

At first I found the collectables a bit annoying, but you don't need most of them to get the important upgrades. I ended up getting everything anyway. I felt It detracted from the classic fps formula at first, but that faded quickly and I actually started having fun hunting them down.

I enjoyed the story as well, even though I didn't buy game for it, but I was pleasantly surprised despite knowing an endgame spoiler.

Performance is great using the Vulkan API and stability was pretty good, I've only had 3 crashes in 35 hours and one of them was probably my fault for rapidly alt-tabbing during loading.

The SnapMap part of it was interesting. I played one or two pretty straight forward campaigns, hopefully there are more interesting ones out there. It reminded me slightly of L4D2's custom maps. I said slightly because L4D2's custom content scene is probably much larger and varied.

Playing multiplayer feels like a good arena shooter, not sure how balanced it is, since I haven't played too much of it, but even without it, the game is worth it.
Especially now (1 July 2020) since it's on sale (-70%).

12 August 2020 Edit:

I played more multiplayer, it was very fun, and to my surprise... still alive, even though if you play frequently enough you start to notice that you're playing with and against the same rather small pool of players in the Team Play mode, however I rarely had to wait for players for a match to start.
The opposite is true for the Free For All mode, which is essentially dead as far as I've seen, every time I tried to play it, the lobby wouldn't start because you need 4 players to start and the most I've seen were 3 total players.

There doesn't seem to be a kick option, so if you get a cheater in your match, you have to either put up with it or leave the match. And depending on the time you get one in your game, if you requeue, chances are you'll be put back in the server you just left, having no other options than to either wait or change the server region setting. 
The game feels decent playing from Eastern Europe on North American and European servers. I haven't tried the other regions.

Thankfully, I've only seen one speed "hacker" thus far.

Also there doesn't seem to be any autobalance system, so if no new player connect you're stuck in 1 vs, 4 scenarios etc..

The gameplay itself is nice, your equipment, runes and weapons being limited until you get to level 50 the first time (you've got a prestige/echelon system, but you keep everything as you progress).

Leveling is pretty fast, especially if you do well in matches. 
Unlocking cosmetics is a chore, sadly, especially if you want to get all the achievements, two of them being particulary grindy. 
The achievements in question are "Computing with Style" and "Beauty is Pain", requiring you to get Echelelon V and VIII, respectively, and then doing some challenges that only become accessible when you've reached those to levels. Even if you meet the criteria before, it won't count.
Alternatively, you have to reach higher levels if you don't complete the challenges, the last one requiring Echelon X.
The challenges aren't very difficult and I've done both soon after I've reached the minimum required level.
